newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia ex-communists back EU but not NATO.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia ex-communists back EU but not NATO.

text.p: Slovenia's pro-Europe former communists, who quit the ruling coalition early this year, said on Monday the tough economic decisions needed for European Union membership should not lead to deep welfare cuts.

The United List of Social Democrats (ZLSD), led by former senior communist official Janez Kocijancic, is hoping that general elections on November 10 will bring it more than the 14 seats it currently holds in Slovenia's 90-member parliament.
Kocijancic said Slovenia would continue its drive to join the EU by the year 2001 whatever the outcome of the nation's second free poll since it declared independence from former Yugoslavia in 1991.
"This process cannot be stopped as there are no alternatives. Slovenians do not want to go back to the Balkans," Kocijancic told Reuters in an interview.
The party split with Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek's ruling coalition in January when the government pushed for the sacking of a United List cabinet minister.

Kocijancic was lukewarm towards Slovenia's prospects of joining NATO. The country has emerged as one of the frontrunners to join the military alliance next year with Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary.
"NATO is not the only alternative. The other is neutrality like in Austria, Sweden and Ireland. We have to know NATO's conditions first and then hold a referendum on the issue," he said.

Kocijancic said his party supported a free market economy with a social face, but acknowledged that public spending had to be curtailed within the next four years to make Slovenia eligible for EU membership.
"We want to retain a high level of social rights in Slovenia and establish a better welfare state," he said.
Kocijancic argued that Slovenia could avoid a fall in benefits for pensioners and the unemployed, and protect low-paid workers with a minimum wage.
"Welfare benefits are not the only thing that draw on the state purse. We have an inefficient state administration and should cut costs in areas like defence and the police," Kocijancic said.
He decried the high level of unemployment, currently at around 13.5 percent, and said a new government should concentrate on boosting education and training.

Latest opinion polls give the United List around five percent voter support, compared with 15.6 percent at the last election in 1992. But with up to 50 percent of the electorate still undecided the poll result is far from certain.
